title: Increasing extreme winds challenge offshore wind energy resilience

paper_content.abstract: Climate change is amplifying the intensity of extreme strong winds, threatening the development and resilience of offshore wind energy systems. The ability of wind turbines to endure such conditions is determined by the fifty-year return period wind speed (U 50), a key parameter for turbine design. However, the long-term trends and spatial variability of U 50 across global oceans remain largely unexplored. Here, we utilize hourly ERA5 wind speed data at 100 meters above sea level from 1940 to 2023 to reveal a significant global increase in oceanic U 50 of 0.016 ms⁻¹ yr-1 (p < 0.01), with upward trends evident in 62.85% of coastal regions. Notably, over 40% of both commissioned and planned offshore wind farms in Asia and Europe have encountered wind speeds exceeding the design threshold of Class III turbines (37.5 ms⁻¹). More than half of these wind farms are situated in regions with increasing U 50 trends, a pattern strongly associated with changes in tropical and extratropical cyclone activity under global warming. These findings underscore the critical need to adapt offshore wind energy infrastructure to withstand evolving wind extremes.
paper_content.introduction:
Offshore wind energy is a cornerstone of the global transition to renewable energy, with cumulative capacity expected to rise from 63 GW in 2022 to nearly 494 GW by 2030 (refs. 1,2). However, offshore wind farms operate in some of the most challenging environments, facing strong winds, waves, and ocean currents 3. Many high-potential offshore wind regions, such as China, Japan, and the United States, are located in cyclone-prone areas, raising concerns about the resilience of offshore wind infrastructure 4.

Recent studies reveal that extreme strong wind events over global oceans are intensifying under climate change. Strong tropical cyclones (TCs), particularly those with lifetime-maximum wind speeds above the 70th percentile of all recorded tropical cyclones, have shown a significant upward trend in maximum wind speed 5. In addition, extratropical cyclones (ETCs) are shifting poleward in both hemispheres 6, with transient eddy kinetic energy showing a pronounced increase along the winter storm tracks in the Southern Hemisphere 7 and a weakening along boreal mid-latitude summer storm tracks 8. Under a warming climate, high-resolution global climate models project both an increase in the frequency of strong TCs (maximum wind speeds exceeding 50 ms-1) and an approximate 3% increase in daily maximum wind speeds of ETCs per degree of warming in high-latitude regions 9–11. These changes are driven by enhanced latent heat flux 12, stronger upper-level winds 13 and shifts in sea surface temperature (SST) patterns 14. This strengthening wind environment threatens the safe operation of wind turbines throughout their multi-decadal lifespans, potentially leading to damage, early retirements, and economic losses 15. For instance, Typhoon Yagi (2024), the strongest autumn typhoon on record, caused the collapse of six wind turbines in Hainan, China and resulted in over US$ 8 million in damages (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Movie 1) 16, highlighting the vulnerability of offshore wind farms to extreme winds.

The parameter used to characterize the maximum wind speed a turbine can endure during its operational lifespan is called the reference wind speed (U ref), which is required to exceed the environmental fifty-year return period wind speed (U 50) at turbine hub height 17. The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) categorizes turbines into Classes I, II, and III, with reference wind speeds of 50, 42.5, and 37.5 ms⁻¹, respectively 18. Therefore, U 50 is a key parameter for assessing extreme wind conditions that are significant for wind turbine design. Normally, U 50 is derived from a Gumbel distribution, requiring long-term observational data for accurate estimation. However, sparse in-situ measurements 19 and the low temporal resolution and inconsistencies of satellite-derived wind products 20,21 limit the robustness of U 50 assessment. Consequently, long-term and spatially homogeneous reanalysis datasets, such as ECMWF’s ERA5 that provides historical wind speed data dating back to 1940, have been extensively used for U 50 estimation 17,22. However, the pattern and magnitude of U 50 changes remain poorly understood under the evolving and predominantly intensifying extreme wind environment, particularly in regions where offshore wind farms are operating or under development. Assessing whether existing and future turbines can endure changing wind extremes is essential for effective offshore wind energy planning and operations.

Here, we present a comprehensive analysis of the long-term trends and spatial variability of U 50 across global oceans from 1940 to 2023. U 50 is estimated by fitting a Gumbel distribution of annual maximum wind speeds over multi-decadal window (>20 years) to ensure robustness 17, with trends analyzed by shifting the time window year by year (see Methods for details). Considering the systemic underestimation of extreme wind speeds in reanalysis datasets caused by grid smoothing 23, we apply a spectral correction method to recover the missing variability in the high-frequency spectrum of wind speed. Since SST is a key indicator of global warming, we examine its relationship with U 50 changes to assess the influence of climate change. We exclude land areas from our analysis because U 50 values over land are significantly lower than the IEC design thresholds, with a spatial average of just 22.57 ms⁻¹ (Supplementary Fig. 2). Our primary aim is to assess risks to offshore wind farms by comparing U 50 values with IEC standards, focusing on both commissioned wind farms and development zones, especially in developing countries with abundant offshore wind potential but limited financial and technical capacity to harness this resource 24. By providing a detailed understanding of the evolving patterns of extreme wind over space and time, we aim to help developers and policymakers reduce investment risks and mitigate potential losses in regions experiencing significant increases in U 50.
paper_content.results:
Extreme wind speed and trends over the ocean
U 50 values in oceanic regions range from below 10 ms-1 to over 50 ms-1, with higher values predominantly occurring along tropical cyclone-prone tracks 25 and in high-latitude regions, especially the Northeastern Pacific, North Atlantic, and Southern Westerlies (Fig. 1a). Our analysis shows that 36.7% of global oceanic grid cells have U 50 values exceeding the U ref of a Class III wind turbine (37.5 ms-1), while approximately 20.2% of grid cells exceed 42.5 ms-1, the U ref for Class II wind turbines (Fig. 1a). Only 0.8% of grid cells surpass 50 ms-1, the U ref associated with Class I wind turbines. For consistency, all U 50 values reported in this study are based on the complete 84-year time series, except for the analysis of U 50 trends derived from the moving time window.

To analyze the spatial distribution of U 50, we classify ocean basins into tropical (5–30°N/S) and extratropical (30–60°N/S) regions, corresponding to the dominant meteorological regimes of TCs and ETCs, respectively. The southern extratropical Atlantic, Pacific and India Ocean are grouped into a unified Southern Westerlies region because they are well-connected and unobstructed by land, resulting in a total of 11 sub-basins (Fig. 1a). The U 50 values in extratropical regions are substantially higher than those in tropical regions. A pronounced right-skewed distribution is observed in the Extratropical North Atlantic (ENA) and Southern Westerlies (SW) regions, indicating a higher frequency of extreme wind events (Fig. 1b). In tropical regions, U 50 values are higher in the Pacific Ocean, with a broader distribution in the Tropical Northwest Pacific (TNWP) and a concentrated right-skewed distribution in the Tropical Northeast Pacific (TNEP). This spatial pattern aligns with the expansive cyclone-prone zone in the TNWP and the frequent occurrence of intense cyclones in the TNEP (Supplementary Fig. 3). These patterns are consistent with those observed in altimeter data 26 and reanalysis dataset from NCEP’s Climate Forecast System Reanalysis 27.

A general upward trend in U 50 is observed across most ocean regions. Globally, the average oceanic U 50 has increased significantly at a rate of 0.016 ms-1 yr-1 over the 30-year window adopted in this research (p < 0.01, Fig. 1c). Trend analysis using continuous 20-year and 50-year windows yields similar rates of change (0.014 ms-1 yr-1 and 0.013 ms-1 yr-1, respectively), suggesting that the choice of time window does not substantially affect the trend estimate (Supplementary Fig. 4). Spatially, 68.0% of oceanic grid cells exhibit a significant increasing trend, while only 14.01% show a decreasing trend (Fig. 1d). Regionally, the tropical regions, including the Northeast Pacific (TNEP), North Atlantic (TNA), North Indian Ocean (TNI), and South Pacific (TSP), exhibit a relatively high proportion of grid cells with substantial increases in U 50. In these regions, 42.77%, 33.03%, 26.35%, and 45.34% of grid cells exhibit an upward trend exceeding 0.05 ms-1 yr-1 (Fig. 1d).

Although this study primarily examines extreme wind speeds, we also assess trends in mean wind speed to identify regions that exhibit both enhanced wind energy potential and heightened extreme wind risks. The ERA5 dataset reveals a modest but widespread increase in mean wind speeds across most oceanic regions from 1940 to 2023, except for equatorial zones and the northern Indian Ocean (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Importantly, increases in mean wind speeds frequently coincide with intensifying extreme winds, particularly in the eastern tropical Pacific, southeastern Pacific, and Southern Westerlies.

In addition, ERA5 provides hourly 3-second gust wind speed, which enables us to determine the origins of extreme wind—whether from sudden high-wind events or sustained strong winds. A significant widening of the difference is observed between gust winds and hourly mean winds (here we use the 90th percentile of the difference as an example), suggesting more frequent sudden high-wind events (Supplementary Fig. 5b). However, spatial discrepancies are observed in the north-central Pacific and northwest Atlantic when comparing ERA5-derived mean wind speed trends with those from altimeter observations 28 and the NCEI blended sea winds product 29. These differences may stem from temporal variations in data coverage, particularly in satellite-based products introduced after 1985.

Extreme wind speed and trend over the coastline
Given that offshore wind farms are primarily sited in coastal regions and that the farthest distance of commissioned wind farms is approximately 100 km from land 30, we specifically extract grid cells within 100 km of the coastline for analysis. In these coastal regions, around 16.49%, 11.25%, and 0.62% of grid cells exceed the reference wind speed thresholds for Class III, Class II, and Class I wind turbines, respectively. The coasts of Canada, England, Japan, and southern Argentina have the highest proportion of U 50 values exceeding the reference wind speed thresholds of wind turbine (Fig. 2a). Significant increases in extreme wind speeds, defined as trends larger than 0.05 ms-1 yr-1, are concentrated in tropical and subtropical coastal zones, including the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean, the southern and eastern United States, India, Southeast Asia, and northern Australia (Fig. 2b). Coastal regions experiencing increasing mean wind speed and concurrently strengthening extreme winds exhibit greater potential for offshore wind energy development, but also face heightened risks, such as the coasts of California, northern and eastern Europe, the Taiwan Strait, Africa, South America, and Australia (Fig. 2b, c). Conversely, concurrent declines in both mean and extreme wind speeds are detected in the Mediterranean Sea, East China, and coastal India, likely associated with the weakening and poleward shift of boreal mid-latitude storm tracks 8.

The risk assessment for fully commissioned offshore wind farms
Changes in extreme oceanic winds pose increasing risks to offshore wind farms. To assess these risks, we categorize wind farms into three risk categories based on the U 50 values of the grid cells in which they are located. These categories correspond to IEC reference wind speed thresholds: Type 1 (U 50 exceeding 37.5 ms⁻¹), Type 2 (U 50 exceeding 42.5 ms⁻¹), and Type 3 (U 50 exceeding 50 ms⁻¹), as winds exceeding these thresholds endanger turbines in each respective category. Fully commissioned offshore wind farms are predominantly located in Europe and Asia, with 136 and 157 wind farms, respectively, and with total installed capacities of 28.86 GW and 25.24 GW 31. Our analysis focuses on U 50 values and their trends at these wind farm locations. Notably, given the large spatial coverage of 0.25° × 0.25° grid cells, multiple wind farms may be situated within the same or neighboring grid cells.

In Europe, U 50 values across commissioned wind farms are closely clustered around the mean of 40 ms-1. The majority of these wind farms (74.26%) are located in regions exhibiting increasing U 50 trends, particularly in key areas such as southeastern UK and the coastal waters of Germany, Denmark, Netherlands, Belgium, and Sweden (Fig. 3a). Specifically, 48 wind farms (total capacity of 9.68 GW) are exposed to Type 1 risk, while 61 wind farms (total capacity of 18.14 GW) face Type 2 risk. Among these high-risk farms, 75.23% are located in regions where U 50 is trending upward. A temporal analysis shows a sharp increase in U 50 around 1975, followed by a temporary decline during 2005–2015, and a renewed upward trend in the past decade (Supplementary Fig. 6a).

In contrast, commissioned wind farms in Asia exhibit greater spatial variability in U 50, with values ranging from below 15 ms-1 to above 40 ms-1 (Fig. 3b). Over half of these sites show decreasing U 50 trends, with spatial variance nearly ten times greater than that observed in Europe. Fewer wind farms are currently at risk in Asia, with eight sites falling under Type 1 risk and two wind farms near the Taiwan Strait exposed to both Type 2 and Type 3 risks (total capacity of 1.45 GW). Among these risk-exposed Asian wind farms, U 50 generally shows an upward trend, though it was briefly interrupted around 1985. However, two wind farms located in South China deviate from this pattern, with trends remaining persistently flat or negative (Supplementary Fig. 6b).

The risk assessment for offshore wind farm development zones
The U 50 values and their trends exhibit broadly similar patterns across offshore wind farm development zones. In Europe, U 50 trends are predominantly characterized by significant increases (68.03% of grid cells), mainly concentrated in the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, and along the west coast of England. Conversely, declining U 50 values are primarily observed along the coastlines of Spain and Italy (Fig. 4a). Among the planned wind farms, 208 are exposed to Type 1 risk, while 292 face Type 2 risk, corresponding to a combined maximum planned capacity of 403.00 GW. Of these, 76.80% are located in areas with rising U 50 trends. The temporal evolution of U 50 across these wind farms mirrors the pattern observed in commissioned wind farms, characterized by a general upward trend interrupted by a temporary decline during 2005–2015 (Supplementary Fig. 7a).

In Asia, 61.23% of planned wind farms are located in regions with increasing U 50 trends, particularly concentrated in South Korea, Vietnam, the eastern and southeastern coasts of China (Fig. 4b). Although the mean U 50 value in planned wind farms across Asia is approximately 4 ms⁻¹ lower than that in Europe, several projects in Asia are exposed to higher risk categories. Specifically, 72 wind farms (total maximum planned capacity of 56.89 GW) face Type 1 risk, 46 wind farms (total maximum planned capacity of 42.11 GW) face Type 2 risk, and 69 wind farms (total maximum planned capacity of 40.52 GW) face Type 3 risk (Fig. 4b). Over 67% of these projects are located in regions where U 50 is increasing. The temporal trends follow a similar pattern to those in Europe, showing a sustained decline prior to the 1990s followed by a rebound after the 1990s (Supplementary Fig. 7b).

There are a total of 172 planned wind farms in North America, South America, and Australia. They are primarily located along the eastern and western coasts of the United States, the northeastern and southeastern coasts of Brazil, and the southwestern and southeastern coasts of Australia (see Supplementary Fig. 8) 31. The increasing trends of U 50 are most pronounced in the northeastern United States and in southeastern and southwestern Australia, while most other sites show decreasing trends. Compared to Europe and Asia, these regions display smaller magnitudes of U 50 trends. In the United States, more than half of the planned wind farms, with a total maximum planned capacity of 50.31 GW, are exposed to Type 1 and Type 2 risks. A substantial increase in U 50 began to emerge around 2005 and has continued to date. The remaining sites fall within a relatively low-risk range for extreme wind (Supplementary Fig. 9).

The U 50 details in developing countries
Given the critical role of developing countries in the global energy transition and in meeting the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 7 to ensure access to clean and affordable energy for all, we analyze extreme wind conditions in nine emerging offshore wind markets, including Brazil, Colombia, India, the Philippines, Romania, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Turkey, and Vietnam 24. These countries have set ambitious targets for offshore wind development, which will require substantial financial commitments. For example, Colombia is planning 12 projects with a total capacity of 5 GW, scheduled for commissioning between 2032 and 2034 (refs. 32,33). India has issued tenders for offshore wind zones targeting 37 GW by 2030, with the transmission system for 10 GW estimated to cost around 0.28 lakh crore (approximately US$ 3.36 billion) 31. Vietnam aims for 6 GW by 2030, with foundation construction alone requiring investments of US$ 40–100 million 24. Brazil has advanced regulatory decrees to facilitate the legal use of offshore areas for wind projects 32. These developments underscore the need for accurate assessments of extreme wind risk to support efficient capital deployment in these countries.

Six of these nine countries, excluding Brazil, Turkey, and Romania, have over half of their coastal grid cells showing increasing U 50 trends. In Turkey, U 50 trends exhibit clear regional variations, with a significant downward trend observed near the Mediterranean Sea and upward trends near the Black Sea (Fig. 2b). In Sri Lanka, over 30% of grid cells show a trend greater than 0.05 ms-1 yr-1 (Fig. 5a). Colombia experiences different oceanic environments due to its exposure to both the Caribbean Sea and the southeastern Pacific Ocean, with extreme winds primarily concentrated along the Caribbean coast (Fig. 2b).

When compared to the reference wind speeds in IEC standards, five countries––South Africa, Vietnam, Turkey, Colombia and the Philippines––will face extreme risks (Fig. 5b). Notably, approximately 3% of coastal grid cells in both Turkey and the Philippines exceed U 50 values of 50 ms⁻¹ (Type 3 risk), with extreme wind conditions in Turkey mainly occurring in the Black Sea. Such high-wind environments pose additional challenges for floating offshore wind energy development, including increased maintenance difficulties and higher anchor costs 34.

Attribution of U 50 trends
To explore potential drivers of the observed changes in U 50, we use the relationship between SST and annual maximum wind speed (AMW), which serves as a proxy for U 50 at annual timescales. While SST is not a direct indicator of wind dynamics, it reflects low-frequency variability in the climate system and may influence storm intensity through thermodynamic and dynamic processes 35. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation (r = 0.80, p < 0.05) between spatially averaged SST and AMW at the global scale from 1940 to 2023 (Fig. 6a). Over this period, AMW increased by 1.05 ms-1 per degree of SST change, indicating a potential response of extreme winds to global warming (Fig. 6b).

The observed correlation between SST and AMW can be explained by the intensification of storm systems under a warming climate. This is because TCs and ETCs account for over 80% of extreme wind events 11,36. Our seasonal analysis indicates that most extreme wind events occur in winter months, suggesting a dominant contribution from ETCs (Supplementary Fig. 10) 37. Regions where extreme winds peak in summer or autumn align with known TC tracks, such as the North Indian Ocean, the tropical Pacific, and the tropical North Atlantic.

Observed changes in cyclone characteristics provide evidence of intensifying wind extremes. The spatial-temporal patterns of cyclone activities derived from best-track data (details refer to Supplementary Methods) are consistent with U 50 changes. Although TC frequency peaked in the 1990s and 2000s, the 2010–2023 period recorded the highest lifetime-maximum wind speeds in most basins (Supplementary Fig. 11a, b). Similarly, accumulated cyclone energy (ACE), defined as ACE = N 0 τ 0 V2 max (where is the maximum wind speed of cyclone, τ is cyclone lifetime, and N is the total number of cyclones) 38, also peaked during this period (Supplementary Fig. 11c). The spatial extent of regions experiencing Category 4 and 5 cyclones (V max larger than 58 ms-1) has expanded by 4.3% compared to the 1980–2001 baseline, particularly in the North Atlantic, consistent with the sharp increase in U 50 observed in the Gulf Stream region (Supplementary Fig. 3). ETCs in both hemispheres are shifting poleward, with notable intensification over the northeastern Atlantic in the Northern Hemisphere and near 60°S in the Southern Hemisphere 11. Storm activities have weakened in midlatitude regions, consistent with the decreasing U 50 trends around the Mediterranean Sea and China’s Bohai Sea.

Several physical mechanisms may contribute to these changes, including enhanced latent heat flux from rising SST 6,12 and increased positive anomalies of lower-tropospheric potential vorticity 11. For instance, TC intensification rates are reported to be three times higher for TCs generated under marine heatwave (MHW) environments compared to those under non-MHW conditions 12. Additionally, a warming climate intensifies upper-level winds and the meridional temperature gradient 39, further promoting the poleward shift of ETCs 6. While future U 50 projections remain uncertain and require comprehensive Earth System Model evaluations, the observed intensification of U 50 is likely to continue in tandem with warming trends 40.

Discussion and implications
This study presents a comprehensive analysis of global extreme oceanic wind speeds (U 50), their long-term trends, and their potential influences from global warming. Using gridded hub-height wind speed data from ERA5 (1940–2023) corrected for underestimation biases via spectral correction, we find that U 50 has significantly increased across 62.85% of global coastal regions over the past nine decades, with a global average trend of 0.016 ms-1 yr-1. Our results show that over 40% of commissioned and planned wind farms in Asia and Europe are exposed to U 50 levels exceeding IEC design thresholds, and more than 60% are located in regions experiencing rising U 50 trends. The changes in U 50 are closely linked to the evolving patterns of TCs and ETCs associated with global warming. Considering the continuous warming trend, regions with upward U 50 trends require more attention to mitigate damages caused by intensifying extreme wind events.

This study has several limitations. The spectral correction (SC) method applied to AMW increases U 50 by an average of 5.56 ms⁻¹ (Supplementary Fig. 12b). However, the SC method tends to underestimate U 50 in cyclone-prone regions, where original U 50 values are retained and warrants further refinement. While the current assessment reveals many high-risk areas overall, wind risks in these regions remain conservative. For offshore wind farms located in cyclone-prone regions, a more detailed downscaling of extreme wind load assessments is recommended to improve design safety. Due to the limited availability of sufficient long-term observations, direct validation of current U 50 results was not feasible; however, the SC method used here is consistent with that employed by Larsén et al. 23, which demonstrated strong agreement with in-situ measurements of AMW 23. This approach has been successfully applied in prior U 50 assessments 22,41,42. Previous studies employing empirical formulas to correct reanalysis wind speed underestimation are limited by a relatively coarse temporal resolution of 1 hour and a lack of in-situ observations exceeding 25 ms⁻¹ (ref. 29). In contrast, the SC method effectively refines U 50 to a 10-minute resolution, aligning with the IEC standard definition.

This study evaluates U 50 at a hub height of 100 m. However, in practice, turbine heights vary and have steadily increased over the past two decades, averaging 104.03 m in 2020 (ref. 43), with the tallest turbine reaching 185 m in 2024. Using power-law extrapolations, we estimate U 50 at hub heights of 80 m, 120 m, 150 m, and 200 m (Supplementary Fig. 13). Results show that U 50 and associated risk increase consistently with height. For instance, the proportion of grid cells facing Type 1 risk rises from 32.48% at 80 m to 54.28% at 200 m, while Type 3 risk coverage expands tenfold when hub height increases from 100 m to 200 m. Although taller turbines improve energy yield and economic returns 44, they also heighten vulnerability to extreme wind events.

The U 50 distribution and trends revealed in this study offer a reference for offshore wind design. However, turbine standards include more than just fifty-year return period wind speed. Other critical design criteria include extreme wind shear, extreme direction change, and extreme turbulence (IEC 61400-1). There are ongoing debates surrounding IEC standards, such as the load factors in IEC 61400-3 are based on north European climates and may not suit cyclone-prone regions 45,46. In addition, observed wind speed variability in coastal Denmark already exceeds the prescribed extreme turbulence model in the IEC 61400-1 Edition 3 standard 47, highlighting the need to localize design criteria based on regional wind behavior.

Extreme winds, especially from TCs and ETCs, are the leading cause of wind turbine failure, accounting for 54.9% of all reported failures 48. These failures can result in substantial economic losses, with damages ranging from US$ 0.64 million to US$ 6.4 million, depending on turbine type, equivalent to 10% of total investment 48. We recommend using higher design-load-class wind turbines in regions with intensified extreme winds. Additionally, resilience-informed planning is crucial to mitigate losses, limit failure propagation, and accelerate recovery, as the failure of one wind turbine can trigger a chain reaction of failures 49. In scenarios where damage from extreme winds is unavoidable, a “strong column-weak beam” design philosophy is suggested to minimize potential losses, with blades designed to fail first to protect more expensive components such as towers and nacelles 50.

In summary, this study highlights a widespread increase in extreme wind speeds across global oceans, with direct implications for offshore wind farm design, siting, and resilience planning. By quantifying U 50 trends and identifying their spatial patterns, our findings offer actionable guidance for industry stakeholders, especially in vulnerable regions. As tropical and extratropical cyclones continue to evolve under global warming, proactive adaptation, including improved risk modeling, revised design standards, and robust turbine engineering, will be essential to safeguard offshore wind infrastructure and support its long-term expansion.
paper_content.methods:
Long-term, gridded hub-height wind speed dataset
The ERA5 dataset is the fifth iteration of the atmospheric reanalysis dataset developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), spanning the period from 1940 onward 51. With a high spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25°, ERA5 provides hourly estimates of wind speed components alongside various meteorological variables. The assimilation process for ERA5 incorporates an extensive array of in-situ and remote-sensing observations. Specifically for wind speed, ERA5 integrates satellite retrievals from radiance data, in-situ measurements from radar detection, drifting buoys, ship stations, and aircraft observations 52. Distinguished from its predecessors, ERA5 is produced using the latest version of the ECMWF Integrated Forecast System (IFS), featuring enhanced model parameterizations and data assimilation methodologies. These improvements have been validated, demonstrating advancements in capturing wind patterns across global oceans 52,53.

The reliability of ERA5 wind speed data has been established through evaluations, particularly in offshore locations 54. It has widespread application in offshore wind resource estimation and extreme wind speed assessments. Examples include global offshore wind energy resource estimations by Soares et al. 55, assessments of extreme wind speeds in the U.S. 56, and on a global scale 17. In this study, we extract hourly u- and v-components of wind speed data from ERA5, covering the period from 1940 to 2023 and at 100 m above the ground, near the wind turbine hub height. ERA5 is a dataset suitable for resolving U 50 assessments because it provides data close to hub height with higher temporal resolution and sufficiently long records. To explore the differences in U 50 at various hub heights, we apply the power law to extrapolate wind speed to different hub heights as an example (details refer to Supplementary Methods). In this research, we only consider and evaluate wind speed from 85°N to 85°S since ERA5 has been reported to have a negative bias in the u- and v-components at the poles 52. For the coastal regions, a grid cell with a land area of less than 10% is defined as oceanic.

Additionally, ERA5 provides 3-second maximum-averaged wind speed for each hour, which is derived by the IFS from hourly averaged surface stress, surface friction, wind shear, and stability 57. Analyzing gust wind allows us to understand whether extreme wind originates from sustained strong winds or abrupt, intense gusts. Since ERA5 offers gust wind data at 10 m height, it is adjusted to 100 m using the power law (details refer to Supplementary Methods).

Sea surface temperature (SST)
SST is incorporated in this study to examine the relationship between changes in extreme wind and global warming. To maintain consistency, SST data were also obtained from ERA5, which assimilates the HadISST2 dataset before 2007 and OSTIA data thereafter, maintaining spatial and temporal resolutions consistent with wind speed data 57. ERA5 SST data show strong agreement with other datasets regarding the warming rate since the mid-1970s, with minor discrepancies observed between HadISST2 and the more recent HadSST4 over the preceding 10 years. The SST analysis is based on a global spatial average, weighted by latitude (details refer to Supplementary Methods).

Dataset of wind farm locations
Wind farm locations are integral to our risk assessment approach, wherein the U 50 assessment is harmonized with offshore wind farm geographical data to provide a tailored risk evaluation for offshore wind farm development. We utilize information from 4C Offshore Ltd (https://map.4coffshore.com/offshorewind/) 31, a renowned market research and consultancy firm specializing in the offshore wind industry, known for its extensive insights into up to 1800 offshore wind projects. The dataset obtained from “4C Offshore” reports a total of 821, 799, and 184 wind farms in Asia, Europe, and other regions, respectively, encompassing both commissioned and under-development projects. This dataset includes key parameters such as latitude, longitude, area, and turbine model types. Additionally, for each wind farm, the dataset specifies the maximum planned installed capacity, while the final installed capacity may be lower. Supplementary Table 1 highlights information on representative wind farms, detailing location, area, installed capacity, wind turbine types, capital expenditure (CAPEX), and investment per MW in U.S. dollars. The wind turbines in Supplementary Table 1 typically have 2–8 MW capacity, with reference wind speeds varying between 42.5 ms-1 and 70 ms-1, depending on the local extreme wind conditions and investment costs. These wind turbines are manufactured by Siemens, Vestas, Goldwind, and Mingyang Electric, among others. CAPEX ranges from around US$ 10 million to over US$ 1 billion, with an investment per MW of US$ 0.12–0.4 million, aligning with surveys in Angel (2017) 58.

Methodology for annual maximum wind speed correction
Reanalysis products such as ERA5 underestimate strong winds due to spatial and temporal averaging effects in the numerical model. These effects lead to reduced spectral energy at high frequency ranges compared to observations, for example, an 11% underestimation of annual maximum wind speed in a numerical model with a grid resolution of 25 km compared to anemometer measurements 23. Larsén et al. 23 developed a spectral correction (SC) method to correct the underestimation by filling the missing variability in the high-frequency range. The observed winds follow a slope of f−5/3 for frequencies f ~ 1 day−1, whereas model-simulated winds exhibit a steeper decay of f−3. The spectral behavior f−5/3 at high frequency is also supported by many theoretical arguments 59,60. This discrepancy arises from energy removal by the model’s dissipation mechanisms, including filtering and damping schemes. Larsén et al. 23 derived this correction using 10-minute observational wind data from Denmark, with the heights ranging between 10 m and 60 m. The correction fc = 0.8 day-1 addresses the underestimated spectral energy occurring at high frequencies (f > 0.8 day-1), while the upper bound fe = 72 day-1 corresponds to the Nyquist frequency of 10-min temporal resolution. Within this frequency range, the wind spectrum S(f) of reanalysis wind is corrected to follow the observed wind spectrum scaling of S(f) = f−5/3. Frequencies outside this range (f < fc or f > fe) remain unaltered. This approach effectively downscales 1-hour ERA5 wind speed data to a 10-minute equivalent resolution, conforming to the IEC standard, which is the recommended temporal resolution for U 50 assessment.

By modeling extreme wind exceedances as a Poisson process, the annual maximum wind speed U max can be derived from the zero- and second-order spectral moments (m 0 and m 2) of the corrected spectrum:
U max = U 0 + sqrt(m 0 / 2π) * sqrt(2ln(sqrt(m 2 / m 0) * T))
where U 0 represents the mean wind speed and T is the reference time period (here T = 1 year). The i-th order spectral moment is defined as:
m i = 2 * integral(f i * S(f) df) from 0 to infinity
where f represents frequency (Hz) and S(f) denotes the wind speed spectrum. For a comprehensive derivation, refer to Larsén et al. 23.

The SC method has been used in different reanalysis products to assess extreme winds globally 22,41,42. However, it systematically underestimates certain regions, especially cyclone-prone regions, as shown by U 50 comparisons between SC-corrected and raw ERA5 data (Supplementary Fig. 13b). This underestimation may stem from stronger cyclone signals in the high-frequency range, where the spectral slope is steeper than f−5/3, which deserves further investigation. While Larsén et al. 22 proposed a modified spectral correction for tropical cyclones (SC-TC), our evaluation found persistent underestimation even after its application. Furthermore, the SC-TC method relies primarily on empirical approximations derived from the Holland model by Ott (2005) 61, rather than direct validation against observational data in tropical cyclone regions. Given these limitations, our study employs the standard SC method for annual maximum wind speed derivation. For cases where the corrected U 50 remains underestimated, the original ERA5 values are retained as conservative estimates.

Methodology for U 50 assessment
Wind speed in regions abundant with wind resources has been shown to follow a two-parameter Weibull distribution with an exponential tail in the strong wind component, as established by previous studies 62,63. Consequently, the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of extreme wind inferred from the Weibull distribution exhibits a double exponential structure with two parameters, α and β, collectively referred to as the Gumbel distribution 64. The formula for the CDF is as follows:
P(U max; α, β) = e^(-e^(-(U max - β) / α))
where U max is the annual maximum wind speed derived from the SC method. The fifty-year return period wind speed (U 50) is the value of U max where the CDF of the Gumbel distribution equals 0.98. The rearrangement of the CDF formula allows us to derive U T at the T-year return period based on the following equation:
U T = -α * ln(-ln(1 - 1/T)) + β

Pryor and Barthelmie (2021) 17 employed four methods to estimate the parameters of the Gumbel distribution, including the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), method of moments (MoM), parameters extrapolated from the Weibull distribution estimation (Gumbel-Weibull), and a graphical method. Among these, MLE is considered one of the most robust non-parametric iterative approaches 65,66, determining parameters by maximizing the likelihood function under the assumed Gumbel distribution 67. MoM, while less computationally demanding, is less robust as α and β can be derived from algebraic functions without iteration. The graphical method involves a linear fitting between the ordered observations and the corresponding probability densities, offering a simplified method for distribution inspection 68 and useful for testing whether the sample of annual maxima is drawn from a single Gumbel distribution 69. These approaches focus on the annual maximum wind speed, requiring data periods longer than 20 years for stable and convincing estimates 70.

The Gumbel-Weibull method first derives the parameters of the Weibull distribution using all available hourly data and then calculates α and β based on a linking function 17. This method is suitable when long-term wind speed data are lacking, as the Weibull distribution parameters can remain relatively stable even with short periods (<10 years). However, results from the Gumbel-Weibull method may show discrepancies, especially in tropical regions 17. In light of these considerations, the MLE method is the preferred choice due to its robustness and reliability, even though it involves higher computational demand.

Trend analysis of extreme wind speed
In the context of escalating extreme wind conditions in coastal and oceanic regions, exploring the changes in U 50 is imperative, as this directly impacts the seamless operation of existing offshore wind farms and the strategic planning of new installations. Leveraging the comprehensive ERA5 dataset, which spans 84 years (1940–2023), we have a valuable opportunity to derive robust estimations of U 50 under various climate conditions. For estimating U 50, previous studies recommend datasets of at least 20 years to ensure sufficient sampling of extreme events. While a 50-year period would theoretically align perfectly with the return period definition, this duration may mask temporal variability and provide fewer samples for trend detection. Finally, U 50 is calculated using overlapping 30-year windows shifted annually. To elaborate, the initial U 50 value is based on data from 1940 to 1969, and the last U 50 value spans from 1994 to 2023, resulting in a total of 55 derived U 50 values. The trend analysis of U 50 is conducted through linear regression applied to these derived values. To validate that the significant changes in U 50 are not contingent on the specific duration of the dataset, we also conduct trend analyses for U 50 derived from continuous 20, 30, and 50-year datasets (Supplementary Fig. 4).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: This paper conducted a detailed analysis of the spatial variability of 50-year-return-period (U_50) high extreme winds over the Earth's oceans to attempt to document their likely risk to offshore wind energy infrastructure. While a global atlas of U_50 is crucial and the results and the attempt are novel, the manuscript is confused about the scope of the work. The problem statement in the Introduction section is quite jumbled. Still, to the best of my understanding, this was the ultimate problem statement that the authors make: "While reanalysis datasets, such as ECMWF’s ERA5, provide valuable historical wind speed records dating back to 1940, previous studies have remained limited to assessing U50 without considering whether significant changes have occurred in the context of climate change". This makes the reader think that the paper will analyze U_50 from the reanalysis record (which it does) and connect it to recent climate change (which it doesn't, even after claiming it to be the shortcoming of earlier studies). To my understanding, the work quantifies the historical risk from extreme high winds using one dataset for one height and then uses that result (without providing any justification or uncertainty estimate) to project the historical risk into the future. This is a serious leap of faith. The paper in the Conclusion section touches on the fact that extreme high winds are not the only factor in the decision- making for wind farms while highlighting other variables that might be considered. Of these factors, the one thing that could have been easily included was the central value (mean/median) of the WSPD distribution. If both mean/median and U_50 increase, it would point to a certain regime of risk versus the places where U_50 increases but mean/median is stationary. Above all, the "suggestions" that the authors provide at the end of the study are pieced together from other studies. However, there isn't a reasonable laying down of the actionable insights gained from THIS STUDY. While I think the core of the study is reasonably impactful and deserves to be made public, the authors need to reframe the study in a way that justifies their assumptions (e.g., past trends continuing into the future), that they are very specific in their use of terminology (e.g., extreme winds - high or low?) and are cognizant about the limitations of their results (e.g., only one hub-height, only one dataset, the uncertainties of that dataset, etc.). This will require a significant amount of re-thinking, re- framing and rewriting, and possibly including a figure of a global map showing the spatial variability of high wind speed risks. I think that such an amount of work likely won't be possible during a manuscript review. So, I would advise the authors to resubmit after significant revisions. I have attached more detailed comments in the text document.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The manuscript "Increasing extreme winds challenge offshore wind energy resilience" by Y. Zhao, Y. Tao, Y. Chen, and Z. Zeng addresses an important problem of shifting climatological norms under anthropogenic climate change. This study has its focus on the 50 years return wind speed, U50, at 100 m above the ground. The design of this study is justified by the needs of the win energy sector. The data analysis procedures are justified by the recommendations of the International Electrotechnical commission. The authors of the study have reported scientifically sounded, methodologically robust, and generally noteworthy results. Assessing the study from the bird-fly altitude, the study looks significant, reliable, and perhaps potentially useful. There are however certain difficulties in the study that need resolutions or at least discussion. The major drawback of the study is that it completely ignore any related physical issues. (a) The study does not differentiate between winds generated in extra-tropical and in tropical circulation systems. Extreme winds related to frontal system of extra-tropical cyclones have different generation mechanism, different effects, constrains, and therefore different statistics as compared to winds generated by convection in tropical storms. Moreover, the selected large regions include both tropical and extra-tropical areas which belong to different circulation systems with different directions of changes in extreme winds. To my opinion, such a physically careless selection of geographical regions for the results' aggregation makes this aggregation less robust for practical applications. (b) The study does not include any discussion of wind gusts. Indeed, there is a discussion of the spectral wind damping in ERA-5 data, but the proposed (in ref 37) correction has not been applied. I see this lacune as a significant gap in the study. Arguably, strong wind gusts could be more damaging for the infrastructure than strong but steady winds. (c) When assessed against previous studies of the same authors, the results of this study look somewhat confusing. Z. Zeng and co-authors have previously reported a reversal of global wind stilling. They found that before 2010 winds over lands were getting more calm. The supplement of this paper (Fig. S2) reports that extreme winds have been increasing all the time since 1970s. What is the cause of such an inconsistency? Tricks of statistical analysis? Data pre-selection? In any case I would like to see the global maps of the mean wind speed, U50, as well as their trends to be sure that the datasets still reproduce the earlier results of the same authors. Pay attention that Fig 3 gives U50 and U50 trends but there is something with color scales. There is no red color on the colorbars for the panels (a) and (b). (d) I have problems with assessing results in Fig. 4. To my view, the color scale clearly shows that large majority of wind parks experience reduction (negative) U50 trends. Nevertheless, the authors report the positive trends, i.e., increased extremes in all regions. Is this related to statistical tricks? The way how the wind park sites weighted and selected? (e) Finally, the part related to country scale analysis demonstrated the weakest relation to the physics and dynamics of the atmosphere. E.g., Turkey has two coastlines - one in the Mediterranean and another in the Black Seas. They are characterized by different wind climates. Mixing them together gives non-observable statistical mean. I would recommend to exclude this so-called country-scale aggregation of U50 from the paper entirely. There are a few less significant problems with the study that worth to mention: (1) The considered distance from the shore is 100 km. However the depth of the ocean is not taken into account. In the shallow North Sea, for example, the wind farms are placed at much larger than 100 km distances offshore, whereas along the dee Norwegian coastal waters, there are no prospects for offshore wind farms. (2) Although ERA-5 reanalysis is the state-of-the-art product, its quality varies depending on the amount of assimilated data. In the areas, like the North Sea, covered with data for a long period, the trends could be robust, but over other regions, there have improved only in XXI century with better satellite data coverage. The implications of data coverage for trend analysis must be discussed in the paper. Despite of the noted drawbacks and lack of physics in the analysis, I consider this study as strong enough to recommend its publication after the required revision. The analysis supports the conclusions, but special reservations are needed when the country-scale conclusions are presented. There are no significant flaws as such but more careful selection of statistically and dynamically homogeneous regions is needed int he revisited version. Statistical and dynamical homogeneity must be demonstrated through, e.g., a cluster analysis or similar procedures. The paper includes enough information to reproduce the results in general. However, the open access code of this paper does not allow to reproduce the results as it requires a number of data files which are no in open access.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The work presented in this manuscript provides valuable insights into wind-energy-relevant extreme wind speeds over oceans. Using ERA5 reanalysis data, the study finds that 50-year-return wind speeds (U50) near hub height have increased over the past decades in many areas, which impacts the design of offshore wind turbines. The authors describe their methods of extracting a trend of U50 from the 84-year dataset, and put results into perspective of wind turbine design requirements. Related literature focuses on extreme winds from reanalysis and satellite data, but the trend of extreme winds has not yet been studied at large scales. Extrapolating the derived trends provides insights into future hub-height offshore wind extremes, supporting the planning of offshore wind energy. Below, I outline a few remarks, mainly about additional details of the methodology. General comments • In addition to the three wind turbine classes discussed in the manuscript, IEC 61400-1 (2019) includes wind turbine class T for areas with moderate wind climates that may experience very high extreme winds (e.g. tropical cyclones), with a reference wind speed (Vref) of 57 m/s. It would be interesting to extend the discussion of Vref vs. U50 for this turbine class as well. • ERA5 is known to underestimate wind speeds in general (not just derived extremes), and a recent paper showed this underestimation for strong ERA5 offshore winds in the context of wind energy (https://wes.copernicus.org/articles/9/7/2024/wes-9-1727-2024.html). This should be included in the discussion. Specific comments Introduction: o L. 47-51: Include a sentence about how U50 and Vref are connected. o L. 57: The resolution of multi-satellite products is comparable to reanalysis products. A major downside of satellite wind products is that they can only provide near-surface winds. A recent study did a similar trend analysis of offshore near-surface winds from satellite data: https://doi.org/10.1175/JTECH-D-24-0008.1 Methods: o Include a brief discussion on how the height of 100m winds in ERA 5 relates to current and future turbine hub heights. o In the IEC standards, both Vref and U50 refer to 10-minute averages. In contrast, ERA5 provides hourly instantaneous values of the 100m winds. A brief discussion about how the different time steps impact results would be helpful. o L. 460: It might be helpful to mention why some wind farms have a higher reference wind speed than the ones mentioned for the turbine classes. o L. 469: Is the CDF derived from the Weibull distribution or from (yearly) maximum values? o L. 479-497: All methods are briefly explained, except the one that is used (MLE). Please add some details about this method. Results: o When discussing the current spatial distribution (not the trend) of U50, could you mention which analysis time period this refers to? o How is Fig. 3a different from Fig S3? o It might be helpful to consistently use units of either m/s/year or m/s/decade. o L. 133-136: This motivates what has already been described in the paragraph above, if I understand correctly. o L. 143: Why is the risk classification based on the turbine class III (lowest) reference wind speed? • L. 242: In the conclusions, it might be helpful to list a global coastal average in addition to a global oceanic average, because of its relevance to wind energy. Technical comments • Fig. 2 c and d both show the trend. Could similar colors be used, maybe throughout all figures in the manuscript showing the same parameter? • L. 131: “Researchers have found” sounds awkward. • L. 304: coastal Denmark • L. 501 and below: I am not sure if “mutations” is the right word here. • Caption Fig. S1: omit “oceanic”

Methodology for annual maximum wind speed correction on page 18
Reanalysis products such as ERA5 underestimate strong winds due to spatial and temporal
averaging effects in the numerical model, leading to reduced spectral energy at high
frequency ranges compared to observations, such as the 11% underestimation of annual
maximum wind speed in a numerical model with a grid resolution of 25 km compared to
anemometer measurements43. Larsén et al43 developed a spectral correction (SC) method to
correct the underestimation by filling the missing variability of high frequency range of
model output. As illustrated in the spectral domain in Larsén et al (also see example from
ERA5 in Supplementary Fig. 11a), observed wind speeds follow a slope of f−5/3 for
frequencies f ~ 1 day−1, whereas model-simulated winds exhibit a steeper decay of f−3. The
spectrum behavior f−5/3 at high frequency is also supported by many theoretical
arguments62,63. This discrepancy arises from energy removal by the model’s dissipation
mechanisms, including filtering and damping schemes. They used observational wind data
from Denmark, with observation heights varying between 10 m and 60 m and recorded every
10 minutes. The correction is applied within a targeted frequency range [f , f ], where the
c e
lower bound f = 0.8 day-1 addresses the underestimated spectral energy occuring at high
c

𝑓−5/3. Frequencies outside this range (f < f or f > f ) remain unmodified. This approach
c e
effectively downscales 1-hour ERA5 wind speed data to a 10-minute equivalent resolution,
which is the recommended temporal resolution for U assessment in the IEC standard.

Reanalysis products such as ERA5 underestimate strong winds due to spatial and temporal
averaging effects in the numerical model, leading to reduced spectral energy at high
frequency ranges compared to observations, such as the 11% underestimation of annual
maximum wind speed in a numerical model with a grid resolution of 25 km compared to
anemometer measurements43. Larsén et al43 developed a spectral correction (SC) method to
correct the underestimation by filling the missing variability of high frequency range of
model output. As illustrated in the spectral domain in Larsén et al (also see example from
ERA5 in Supplementary Fig. 11a), observed wind speeds follow a slope of f−5/3 for
frequencies f ~ 1 day−1, whereas model-simulated winds exhibit a steeper decay of f−3. The
spectrum behavior f−5/3 at high frequency is also supported by many theoretical
arguments62,63. This discrepancy arises from energy removal by the model’s dissipation
mechanisms, including filtering and damping schemes. They used observational wind data
from Denmark, with observation heights varying between 10 m and 60 m and recorded every
10 minutes. The correction is applied within a targeted frequency range [f , f ], where the
c e

e

S(f) of reanalysis wind is corrected to follow the observed wind spectrum scaling of 𝑆(𝑓) =
𝑓−5/3. Frequencies outside this range (f < f or f > f ) remain unmodified. This approach
c e
effectively downscales 1-hour ERA5 wind speed data to a 10-minute equivalent resolution,
which is the recommended temporal resolution for U assessment in the IEC standard.
